segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you yourselves know, brothers and sisters, that our visit to you was not in vain,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but though we had already suffered and been shamefully treated in Philippi, as you know, we found boldness in our God to speak to you the good news of God amid a great struggle.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For our appeal does not come from error or from impure motives, nor is it made with deceit,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: but just as we have been tested and found fit by God to be entrusted with the good news, so we speak, not to please people but to please God, who tests our hearts.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we never came with flattering words, as you know, nor with a cover for greed, God is our witness,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: nor were we seeking glory from people, whether from you or from others,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: though as apostles of Christ we could have made our weight felt. Instead we were gentle among you, like a nursing mother cherishing her own children.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: So, yearning for you, we were glad to share with you not only the good news of God but also our own lives, because you had become so dear to us.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you remember, brothers and sisters, our labor and toil: working night and day so as not to burden any of you, we proclaimed to you the good news of God.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: You are witnesses, and so is God, of how devoutly and justly and blamelessly we behaved toward you who believe,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: just as you know how we dealt with each one of you like a father with his own children,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: appealing to you and encouraging you and solemnly charging you to walk in a manner worthy of God, who calls you into his own kingdom and glory.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: And for this reason we too thank God unceasingly: when you received the word of God that you heard from us, you accepted it not as the word of people but as what it truly is, the word of God, which is also at work in you who believe.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For you, brothers and sisters, became imitators of the assemblies of God in Christ Jesus that are in Judea, because you too suffered the same things from your own compatriots as they did from the Jews

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: who killed both the Lord Jesus and the prophets and drove us out, who do not please God and are opposed to all people,

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: preventing us from speaking to the Gentiles so that they may be saved, so as always to fill up the measure of their sins. But the wrath has come upon them at last.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: But we, brothers and sisters, orphaned from you for a short time—in person, not in heart—made all the greater effort, with great desire, to see your face.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For we wanted to come to you—I, Paul, more than once—but Satan blocked our way.

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: For what is our hope or joy or the crown we will boast of before our Lord Jesus at his coming—is it not indeed you?

segments.speaker: narrator
segments.text: Yes, you are our glory and our joy.

notes.note: The Greek plural was the ordinary way to address a mixed group of men and women, and Paul is writing to the whole community. “Brothers” alone now suggests to many readers that only men are addressed. Several modern translations make the same choice; others keep “brothers” and explain it in a footnote.

The Greek word means “empty.” It may mean the visit was not fruitless, or that it was not hollow—lacking in substance, sincerity, or power. The following verses, which defend the character of the mission, give some support to the second reading; the rendering here follows the more common first one.

The Greek was an ordinary word for a public announcement of good news, used among other things for imperial proclamations. “Gospel” has since become a religious term or the name of a kind of book. Many modern translations already alternate between “good news” and “gospel.”

Literally “been in weight.” The phrase can mean being a financial burden (compare verse 9, where a related verb means “to burden”) or carrying weight in the sense of insisting on one’s importance and authority. The context, which speaks of seeking glory in verse 6 and of gentleness in what follows, slightly favors the second, but both may be in view.

Manuscripts are divided between “gentle” (ēpioi) and “infants” (nēpioi), which differ by a single letter that could easily be doubled or dropped after the preceding word. The earliest manuscripts mostly read “infants,” and some critical editions print it; the edition translated here reads “gentle,” as do most English versions, because it fits the image that follows. The question remains disputed.

The Greek word usually denotes a nurse, often a wet nurse hired to care for another family’s children. Paul specifies “her own children,” so the picture is either of a mother nursing or of a professional nurse giving her own children the tenderest care of all.

The Greek word meant a gathering of people—a city’s citizen assembly, or in the Greek Old Testament Israel gathered before God. “Church” now suggests a building or an institution, so this translation uses “assembly” throughout. “Church” is the near-universal rendering, and readers know what it refers to.

The Greek can be read as limiting (“those Jews who killed…”) or as a description of the whole people (“the Jews, who killed…”); the translation leaves out the comma, taking it as the former. Paul, himself a Jew, is comparing persecution in Thessalonica with what the assemblies in Judea suffered from their own people, and some would translate “Judeans” here. A minority of scholars regard verses 14–16 as a later insertion, though no manuscript lacks them.

The Greek word means “peoples” or “nations.” In the plural, in Jewish usage, it refers to the non-Jewish peoples, and it is translated “Gentiles” in that sense and “nations” elsewhere. It is one word in Greek.

The Greek phrase can mean “at last,” “completely,” “to the end,” or “forever,” and translations differ. It is also unclear what Paul has in mind by wrath having come: a recent calamity, or a future judgment spoken of as certain. Scholars have proposed several events from the late 40s, but none can be confirmed.

notes.traditional: taken from you; torn away from you
notes.note: The Greek verb means to be made an orphan, and it could be used more loosely of any painful bereavement, including parents separated from children. It continues the family imagery of the chapter, where Paul has compared himself to a nursing mother and a father.

The Greek word means “arrival” or “presence,” and it was a standard term for the official visit of a king or emperor to a city, an occasion marked by public welcome and honors. Paul uses it for the expected arrival of Jesus as Lord. The “crown” in the same verse is the wreath awarded to a victor or an honored person.

candidates.reason: The plural address to mixed communities recurs throughout the letters and Acts, and translations split between “brothers” and “brothers and sisters.”
The verb and its noun παράκλησις range over appeal, urge, encourage, and comfort across the letters, and need rules for when each English word applies.
The Semitic idiom of “walking” for conduct recurs across Paul and John, and translators vary between “walk” and “live.”
The word covers human reputation or honor as well as divine splendor, and a rule is needed for when “honor” or “praise” replaces “glory.”
“Wrath” versus “anger,” and whether to supply “God’s” where the Greek has only “the wrath,” should be settled once for the whole New Testament.

warnings: Verse 4: πιστεύω is not rendered with a register form (believe / trust) and has no register-exception note.

Verse 8: ψυχή is not rendered with a register form (life; soul; person / people / everyone / human being; living being / living creature; mind; wholeheartedly; keep in suspense) and has no register-exception note.
